body.en: Conic sections are planar curves formed by the intersection of a double right-circular cone with a slicing plane. Equivalently, every non-degenerate conic arises as the locus of points whose ratio of distance from a fixed focus to a fixed directrix line is constant (eccentricity). This chapter establishes the Cartesian standard forms, focus-directrix unifications, general quadratic classifications, axis rotation transformations, and polar conics.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Standard Forms, Completing the Square & Geometric Features

body.en: Master the standard geometric equations for parabolas, ellipses, hyperbolas, and circles, and convert general second-degree equations into canonical form by completing the square.

caption.en: Circle sector and chord geometry with radius r = 6 and central angle 120°.

label.en: Level 1 (Foundations) — Canonical Reduction by Completing the Square

problem.en: Convert the general quadratic equation \(4x^2 + 9y^2 - 16x + 54y + 61 = 0\) to standard canonical form. Identify the conic section, its center, vertices, foci, and eccentricity.

solution.en:
Step 1: Group variables and isolate constants: \[ 4(x^2 - 4x) + 9(y^2 + 6y) = -61. \]

Step 2: Complete the square in both variables: \[ 4(x^2 - 4x + 4) + 9(y^2 + 6y + 9) = -61 + 4(4) + 9(9) = -61 + 16 + 81 = 36. \] \[ 4(x - 2)^2 + 9(y + 3)^2 = 36. \]

Step 3: Normalize to 1 by dividing by 36: \[ \frac{(x - 2)^2}{9} + \frac{(y + 3)^2}{4} = 1. \]

Step 4: Extract geometric invariants:

  • Conic Type: Horizontal Ellipse with \(a^2 = 9 \implies a = 3\) and \(b^2 = 4 \implies b = 2\).
  • Center: \((h, k) = (2, -3)\).
  • Vertices: \((h \pm a, k) = (2 \pm 3, -3) \implies (-1, -3)\) and \((5, -3)\).
  • Focal Distance: \(c = \sqrt{a^2 - b^2} = \sqrt{9 - 4} = \sqrt{5}\).
  • Foci: \((2 \pm \sqrt{5}, -3)\).
  • Eccentricity: \(e = \frac{c}{a} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3} \approx 0.745\).

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Analytical Application — Focus-Directrix Unification & General Quadratic Discriminant

body.en: Unify all conic sections under the focus-directrix-eccentricity ratio definition and classify general second-degree polynomials using the discriminant invariant.

Theorem: Let \(F\) be a fixed point (focus) and \(L\) be a fixed line (directrix) in the plane not containing \(F\). The locus of all points \(P\) such that the ratio of distance to the focus to perpendicular distance to the directrix is a constant \(e > 0\): \[ \frac{d(P, F)}{d(P, L)} = e \] defines a non-degenerate conic section:

  • \(e = 0\): Circle (limiting case where directrix is at infinity).
  • \(0 < e < 1\): Ellipse (closed oval curve).
  • \(e = 1\): Parabola (open curve; equal distance to focus and directrix).
  • \(e > 1\): Hyperbola (two unbounded symmetric branches).

For any general quadratic curve in the plane: \[ Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0, \] the quantity \(\Delta = B^2 - 4AC\) is an algebraic invariant under planar rotation and translation:

Discriminant \(\Delta = B^2 - 4AC\)Conic Section ClassificationGeometric Properties
\(\Delta < 0\) (\(B=0, A=C\))CircleZero eccentricity; equal principal axes
\(\Delta < 0\) (\(B=0, A \ne C, AC > 0\))EllipseClosed bounded curve; \(0 < e < 1\)
\(\Delta = 0\)ParabolaSingle axis of symmetry; \(e = 1\)
\(\Delta > 0\)HyperbolaTwo asymptotic directions; \(e > 1\)

Degenerate Cases: When the polynomial factors into linear components over \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\), the locus degenerates into a single point, two intersecting lines, parallel lines, or the empty set.

label.en: Level 2 (Analytical Application) — Discriminant Classification & Parabolic Focus

problem.en: Classify the curve \(3x^2 - 12x - 8y + 4 = 0\) using the discriminant, convert it to standard form, and find its vertex, focus, directrix line, and focal width (latus rectum).

solution.en:
Step 1: Discriminant check: Here \(A = 3\), \(B = 0\), and \(C = 0\). \[ \Delta = B^2 - 4AC = 0^2 - 4(3)(0) = 0 \implies \text{Parabola}. \]

Step 2: Convert to canonical form: \[ 3(x^2 - 4x) = 8y - 4 \implies 3(x^2 - 4x + 4) = 8y - 4 + 12 = 8y + 8. \] \[ 3(x - 2)^2 = 8(y + 1) \implies (x - 2)^2 = \frac{8}{3}(y + 1). \]

Step 3: Extract parabolic features:

  • Standard form: \((x - h)^2 = 4p(y - k)\) with \((h, k) = (2, -1)\).
  • Focal parameter: \(4p = \frac{8}{3} \implies p = \frac{2}{3} > 0\) (opens vertically upward).
  • Vertex: \((2, -1)\).
  • Focus: \((h, k + p) = \left(2, -1 + \frac{2}{3}\right) = \left(2, -\frac{1}{3}\right)\).
  • Directrix: \(y = k - p = -1 - \frac{2}{3} \implies y = -\frac{5}{3}\).
  • Latus Rectum (focal width): \(|4p| = \frac{8}{3}\).

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced / University Rigor — Axis Rotation & Polar Conics

body.en: Eliminate cross-product xy terms by rotating coordinate axes and analyze planetary orbits and satellite trajectories using polar conics centered at the focal pole.

label.en: ● Elimination of the Cross-Product xy Term via Axis Rotation

body.en:
Theorem: To eliminate the \(Bxy\) cross-product term in \(Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0\), rotate the Cartesian coordinate axes through an angle \(\theta\) satisfying: \[ \cot(2\theta) = \frac{A - C}{B} \quad (0 < 2\theta < \pi). \] If \(A = C\), then \(\cot(2\theta) = 0 \implies 2\theta = 90^\circ \implies \theta = 45^\circ\).

The coordinate transformation equations are: \[ x = x'\cos\theta - y'\sin\theta, \qquad y = x'\sin\theta + y'\cos\theta. \] Substituting into the quadratic yields an equation in the rotated system \((x', y')\) of the form \(A'(x')^2 + C'(y')^2 + D'x' + E'y' + F = 0\) with \(B' = 0\).

label.en: ● Polar Equations of Conic Sections with Focus at the Pole

body.en:
Theorem: In polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) with a focus at the pole \((0,0)\) and directrix at distance \(d\) from the pole: \[ r = \frac{ed}{1 \pm e\cos\theta} \quad (\text{vertical directrix } x = \pm d), \qquad r = \frac{ed}{1 \pm e\sin\theta} \quad (\text{horizontal directrix } y = \pm d). \]

Derivation: For a vertical directrix at \(x = d\), the distance from point \(P(r,\theta)\) to the directrix is \(d - x = d - r\cos\theta\). By the focus-directrix definition: \[ \frac{r}{d - r\cos\theta} = e \implies r = e(d - r\cos\theta) = ed - er\cos\theta. \] \[ r(1 + e\cos\theta) = ed \implies r = \frac{ed}{1 + e\cos\theta}. \quad \blacksquare \]

label.en: Level 3 (Advanced Rigor) — Axis Rotation & Hyperbolic Asymptotes

problem.en: Consider the equation \(xy = 4\). (a) Use rotation of axes to transform this equation into standard canonical form in the \((x', y')\) system. (b) Identify the conic, its vertices, and its eccentricity.

solution.en:
(a) Rotation of axes: Here \(A = 0\), \(B = 1\), and \(C = 0\). Since \(A = C\), \[ \cot(2\theta) = \frac{0 - 0}{1} = 0 \implies 2\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} \implies \theta = \frac{\pi}{4} = 45^\circ. \] The transformation equations with \(\cos(45^\circ) = \sin(45^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) are: \[ x = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(x' - y'), \qquad y = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(x' + y'). \] Substitute into \(xy = 4\): \[ \left[\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(x' - y')\right] \left[\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(x' + y')\right] = 4 \implies \frac{1}{2}((x')^2 - (y')^2) = 4. \] \[ \frac{(x')^2}{8} - \frac{(y')^2}{8} = 1. \]

(b) Identify conic features:

  • This is an equilateral (rectangular) hyperbola with \(a^2 = 8\) and \(b^2 = 8\).
  • Vertices in rotated system: \((\pm a, 0) = (\pm\sqrt{8}, 0) = (\pm 2\sqrt{2}, 0)\).
  • Vertices in original system: \(x = y = \pm 2\), i.e., \((2, 2)\) and \((-2, -2)\).
  • Eccentricity: \(c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \sqrt{8 + 8} = 4 \implies e = \frac{c}{a} = \frac{4}{2\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}\).

label.en: ⚠️ Common Traps & Exam Pitfalls — Conic Sections

body.en:
• Ellipse vs. Hyperbola Pythagorean Relations: For an ellipse, \(c^2 = a^2 - b^2\) (foci are inside the curve, so \(c < a\)). For a hyperbola, \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\) (foci are outside the vertices, so \(c > a\)). Conflating these two formulas is the most prevalent conic error.
  • Hyperbola Orientation & Value of a: In an ellipse, \(a\) is always the larger semi-axis (\(a > b\)). In a hyperbola, \(a^2\) is strictly the denominator of the positive term, regardless of whether \(a > b\), \(a < b\), or \(a = b\).
  • Completing the Square with Factored Coefficients: In expressions like \(4(x^2 - 4x)\), adding \(4\) inside the parenthesis actually adds \(4 \times 4 = 16\) to the left side. You must add \(16\) (not \(4\)) to the right side to maintain balance.
  • Sign of p in Parabolas: In \((x-h)^2 = 4p(y-k)\), if \(p < 0\), the parabola opens downward; in \((y-k)^2 = 4p(x-h)\), if \(p < 0\), it opens to the left. The focus is always located in the direction the curve opens.

label.en: Worked Example D — Euclidean Distance & Orthogonal Projection

body.en:
A displacement has horizontal component \( \Delta x = 5 \) and vertical component \( \Delta y = 5 \). Find the squared magnitude \( d^2 \) and the area of the right triangle formed with the axes.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. By the Pythagorean theorem, \( d^2 = (5)^2 + (5)^2 = 25 + 25 = \mathbf{50} \).
  2. The enclosed right-triangle area is \( A = \frac{1}{2}(5)(5) = \mathbf{12.5} \).

question.en: Find the vertex, focus, and directrix of the parabola given by the general equation \(y^2 + 8x - 4y + 28 = 0\).

solution.en:
Complete the square on the \(y\)-terms:

\[y^2 - 4y = -8x - 28 \implies (y^2 - 4y + 4) = -8x - 28 + 4.\]\[(y - 2)^2 = -8x - 24 = -8(x + 3).\]

This matches \((y - k)^2 = 4p(x - h)\) with:

  • Vertex: \((h, k) = (-3, 2)\)
  • Focal parameter: \(4p = -8 \implies p = -2\) (opens horizontally to the left)
  • Focus: \((h + p, k) = (-3 + (-2), 2) = (-5, 2)\)
  • Directrix: \(x = h - p = -3 - (-2) \implies x = -1\)

question.en: An ellipse has vertices at \((1, 6)\) and \((1, -4)\), and a focus at \((1, 4)\). Determine its standard equation and compute its eccentricity.

solution.en:
The vertices share \(x = 1\), so the major axis is vertical.

Center is the midpoint of the vertices: \((h, k) = \left(1, \frac{6 + (-4)}{2}\right) = (1, 1)\).

Semi-major axis: \(a = 6 - 1 = 5\) (so \(a^2 = 25\)).

Focal distance from center to \((1, 4)\): \(c = 4 - 1 = 3\).

For an ellipse, \(b^2 = a^2 - c^2 = 25 - 9 = 16 \implies b = 4\).

Standard equation: \[\frac{(x - 1)^2}{16} + \frac{(y - 1)^2}{25} = 1.\]

Eccentricity: \[e = \frac{c}{a} = \frac{3}{5} = 0.6.\]

question.en: [Conic Sections & Analytic Geometry · Practice 3] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 5t + 5 \), evaluate \( g(8) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 50 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 8 \): \( g(8) = 5(8) + 5 = \mathbf{45} \). Setting \( 5t + 5 = 50 \) gives \( 5t = 45 \implies t = \mathbf{9} \).

question.en: [Conic Sections & Analytic Geometry · Practice 4] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 6t + 6 \), evaluate \( g(10) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 72 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 10 \): \( g(10) = 6(10) + 6 = \mathbf{66} \). Setting \( 6t + 6 = 72 \) gives \( 6t = 66 \implies t = \mathbf{11} \).
